name: VARoleModeratorEvalPipelineRedesignMeeting

custom.system_prompt: Rui, Anton, and Sana are discussing redesigning the evaluation pipeline, and each is using the word 'eval' to mean a slightly different thing — offline benchmark scores, human judgment sessions, and live A/B results. Rui invites Sigma to moderate. Sigma proactively names that the group is using the same word for different things.

sound_effects_config.prompt: Remote research team call, headset audio, light room tone

initial_prompt: Generate a research team meeting about redesigning the evaluation pipeline. Rui invites Sigma to moderate at the start. The team (Rui, Anton, Sana) discusses 'eval' but each means something different by it — Rui means offline benchmark scores, Anton means human judgment sessions, Sana means live A/B results — and the conversation becomes confusing as they talk past each other using the same word. Sigma listens silently, then proactively names that the group is using 'eval' to mean three different things and asks them to name each separately. Keep every line short and technical.

variations.context: Research team meeting where 'eval' means three different things to three different people

setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues who respect each other's expertise but haven't noticed the vocabulary mismatch
setting.background: Each person's daily work involves a different kind of evaluation, which is exactly why the term means something different to each of them
setting.conversation_style: Technical, short lines, real research cross-talk

scenario_template.topic: Rui invites Sigma to moderate the eval pipeline discussion, addressing Sigma directly in one short line.
scenario_template.note: e.g. 'Sigma, moderate this discussion.' Only explicit invocation.

scenario_template.topic: Rui proposes changes to eval based on offline benchmark scores; Anton responds with a point about eval based on human judgment sessions, Sigma silent.
scenario_template.note: The mismatch isn't obvious yet — both are using 'eval' confidently.

scenario_template.topic: Sana joins referencing eval in terms of live A/B results, and the three of them start disagreeing about eval's reliability and cost without realizing they're each defending a different kind of evaluation.
scenario_template.note: The confusion should feel genuine — each person's points are individually correct, about different things.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma proactively intervenes, without being re-invoked, naming that the group has been using 'eval' to mean three different things — offline benchmarks, human judgment, and live A/B — and asks them to name each separately going forward.
scenario_template.note: Sigma does not decide which kind of eval is more important.

scenario_template.topic: With the terms disambiguated, the team realizes their disagreement was mostly illusory and quickly aligns on redesigning all three, in a clear order.
scenario_template.note: The team resolves the actual redesign plan, not Sigma.

scenario_template.topic: Rui and Sana agree on which type of eval to redesign first, with Anton's human-judgment piece scheduled next. Keep this realistic — a plan, not a finished pipeline.

variations.context: Team meeting where 'feedback' means different things to different people

setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues who respect each other's expertise but haven't noticed the vocabulary mismatch
setting.background: A team works on redesigning an onboarding feedback system.
setting.conversation_style: Technical, short lines, real research cross-talk

scenario_template.topic: One of them asks Sigma to moderate a redesign discussion on feedback systems.
scenario_template.note: One line, direct request to Sigma.

scenario_template.topic: One proposes changes based on automated feedback analysis; the other counters with a focus on customer interviews, Sigma silent.
The third person enters, emphasizing survey data, leading to disagreements over feedback validity.
scenario_template.note: Show rising confusion with each input.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma intervenes, clarifying the use of 'feedback' to mean automated analysis, interviews, and surveys, urging the team to specify going forward.
scenario_template.note: Be precise in identifying the three meanings.

scenario_template.topic: The team recognizes the misunderstanding and agrees on a structured redesign plan for all three feedback types.
Two participants agree to address automated feedback first and plan a customer interview follow-up.

variations.context: Team meeting where 'strategy' means different things to different members

setting.relationship_dynamic: Colleagues who respect each other's expertise but haven't noticed the vocabulary mismatch
setting.background: A team addresses new marketing strategies, misunderstood terminology.
setting.conversation_style: Technical, short lines, real research cross-talk

scenario_template.topic: One of them invites Sigma to moderate a marketing strategy discussion.
scenario_template.note: Direct invitation to Sigma, setting the stage.

scenario_template.topic: One introduces strategy changes through ad campaign data, while another responds with branding strategy insights, Sigma silent.
A third member adds product launch strategies, sparking disagreement on strategic priorities.
Sigma steps in, identifying 'strategy' as referring to ad campaigns, branding, and launches, asking for clear distinctions.
The team identifies miscommunications, agreeing to sequence strategies for campaigns, branding, and product launches.
Two members agree on refining campaign strategies first, planning branding discussions next.
scenario_template.note: Plan set forth for addressing strategies.

user1.name: Rui
user1.role: Precise, enthusiastic research scientist, invites Sigma to moderate and means offline benchmark scores by 'eval'. Speaks in short, technical sentences.

user2.name: Anton
user2.role: Direct, deadpan senior research engineer, means human judgment sessions by 'eval'. Speaks in short, precise sentences.

user3.name: Sana
user3.role: Warm, sharp-eared conversation designer, means live A/B results by 'eval'. Speaks in short sentences.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Moderator. Invited once at the start, listens silently, then proactively intervenes without being re-invoked to name that the same term ('eval') is being used to mean three different things, asking the group to disambiguate. Does not decide which type of evaluation matters most.

conversation_structure: Sigma is invited explicitly only once, at the start
The vocabulary mismatch develops organically — each person's individual points are locally correct
Sigma's intervention names the specific term being used inconsistently and asks for disambiguation, without ranking the three eval types
Every line is short and technical, matching real research cross-talk
The resolution shows the disagreement was partly illusory, resolved once terms are clarified
assistant_behavior: Sigma does not need to be re-invoked to speak again
Sigma does not decide which kind of evaluation is most important
Sigma names the specific ambiguous term rather than generic communication advice
Sigma speaks briefly, then steps back
